lessons.title: Accuracy and its limits
key_points: Accuracy is the share of predictions that are right: correct predictions divided by all predictions.
A confusion matrix shows where the mistakes are. For two classes it has four cells: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.
Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data. If 95 of 100 emails are not spam, a model that always says "not spam" scores 0.95 and catches no spam at all.
Always compare accuracy with the share of the most common class, and look at the confusion matrix before trusting a single number.
In scikit-learn: accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred) and confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred).

worked_example.title: Read a confusion matrix
steps: A model screens 100 students for risk of failing. 10 are really at risk.
It flags 8 students: 6 really at risk (true positives) and 2 not (false positives).
It misses 4 at-risk students (false negatives). The other 86 are correctly left alone (true negatives).
Accuracy = (6 + 86) / 100 = 0.92. That sounds high, but the model missed 4 of the 10 students it exists to find.
worked_example.code:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, confusion_matrix

y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
print(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred))
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred))  # rows: true class, columns: predicted

mini_project.title: Find where your model is wrong
mini_project.brief: Use the classifier from Machine learning basics, or any classifier you have.
steps: Compute accuracy on the test set.
Print the confusion matrix and label its rows and columns by hand.
Find the pair of classes the model confuses most.
Look at three of those wrong examples and write a guess at why they were hard.
mini_project.done_when: You can name the model's most common mistake and give one likely reason.

lessons.title: Precision and recall
key_points: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of everything the model flagged, how much was right.
Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of everything it should have found, how much it found.
Raising the decision threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall; lowering it does the opposite.

Choose by the cost of each mistake. Missing a sick patient (a false negative) is worse than an extra test, so favour recall. Wrongly blocking a real email (a false positive) annoys users, so favour precision for a spam filter.
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2 × P × R / (P + R). It is high only when both are high.

worked_example.title: Precision and recall for the at-risk screen
steps: Using lesson 1's numbers: TP = 6, FP = 2, FN = 4.
Precision = 6 / (6 + 2) = 0.75. Three of every four flagged students were really at risk.
Recall = 6 / (6 + 4) = 0.60. The model found only 60% of at-risk students.
Missing a student who needs help is the costly mistake here, so you would lower the threshold to raise recall, accepting a few more false alarms.
worked_example.code:
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, classification_report

print(precision_score(y_test, y_pred), recall_score(y_test, y_pred), f1_score(y_test, y_pred))
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))

mini_project.title: Move the threshold
mini_project.brief: See the trade-off with your own numbers.
steps: Train a LogisticRegression on a two-class dataset (for example scikit-learn's breast cancer dataset).
Get probabilities with predict_proba and turn them into predictions at thresholds 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7.
Compute precision and recall at each threshold in a small table.
Pick a threshold for a stated use and explain your choice in two sentences.
mini_project.done_when: Your table shows precision rising and recall falling as the threshold goes up, with a justified choice.

lessons.title: Overfitting
key_points: Overfitting: the model learns the training data, noise included, so it scores much higher on training data than on new data.
Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the pattern, so it scores low on both.
Compare training and test scores. A large gap (for example 1.00 on training, 0.70 on test) is the usual sign of overfitting.
Fixes for overfitting: more data, simpler models, fewer features, regularisation, or limits such as a maximum tree depth.
For regression, measure error with MAE (average absolute error, in the target's own units) or RMSE (penalises large errors more). Lower is better for both.

worked_example.title: See overfitting in a decision tree
steps: Train DecisionTreeClassifier() with no depth limit. Training accuracy is 1.00 because the tree can memorise every row.
Its test accuracy is clearly lower, which shows the gap.
Train again with max_depth=3. Training accuracy drops a little but test accuracy often rises.
Keep the depth that gives the best score on held-out data, not on training data.
worked_example.code:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

for depth in [None, 3]:
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(depth, tree.score(X_train, y_train), tree.score(X_test, y_test))

mini_project.title: Plot the gap
mini_project.brief: Watch overfitting appear as a model gets more complex.
steps: Train decision trees with max_depth from 1 to 15 on one dataset.
Record training and test accuracy for each depth.
Plot both lines on one chart with matplotlib.
Mark where underfitting ends and overfitting starts, and say which depth you would choose.
mini_project.done_when: Your chart shows both lines and you have named a depth with a reason.

lessons.title: Cross-validation
key_points: One train/test split can be lucky or unlucky. k-fold cross-validation splits the training data into k parts, trains k times and tests on each part once.
The result is k scores. Report their mean and spread (standard deviation); a large spread means the score depends on which rows you got.
Use cross-validation on the training set to compare models and choose hyperparameters. Keep the final test set for one last check.
cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5) runs 5-fold cross-validation. For classification it stratifies the folds by default.
GridSearchCV tries each setting you list with cross-validation and keeps the best one.

worked_example.title: Pick k for k-nearest neighbours
steps: For k in 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, run 5-fold cross-validation on the training set.
Print the mean and standard deviation of each set of scores.
Choose the k with the best mean score; if two are close, prefer the one with the smaller spread or the simpler model.
Fit that model on the whole training set and score it once on the test set.
worked_example.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

for k in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]:
    scores = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k), X_train, y_train, cv=5)
    print(k, scores.mean().round(3), scores.std().round(3))

mini_project.title: Choose a model fairly
mini_project.brief: Compare two models the way a team would.
steps: Pick two models, for example LogisticRegression and a DecisionTreeClassifier with max_depth=5.
Run 5-fold cross-validation for each on the training set, choosing a metric that fits your problem (accuracy, recall or F1).
Report mean ± standard deviation for both.
Fit the winner on the full training set and report its test score once, with one sentence on whether it matches the cross-validation result.
mini_project.done_when: You have cross-validation results for two models and a single final test score for the winner.

check.prompt: 99 of 100 transactions are normal. A model always predicts "normal". What is its accuracy, and is it useful for finding fraud?

options.text: 0.99, but it finds no fraud at all

check.explanation: It is right on all 99 normal cases, so accuracy is 0.99, yet it misses the one fraud case. This is why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.

check.prompt: A model flags 20 items; 15 are truly positive. There were 30 positives in total. What are precision and recall?
check.explanation: Precision = 15 / 20 = 0.75 (of the flagged items, how many were right). Recall = 15 / 30 = 0.50 (of all positives, how many were found).

check.prompt: A clinic screen must miss as few sick patients as possible. Which measure matters most?
check.explanation: Missing a sick patient is a false negative. Recall measures how many real positives are found, so it is the one to keep high.

check.prompt: Training accuracy is 0.99 and test accuracy is 0.68. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: The test set is too easy
The labels are all the same

check.explanation: A big gap between training and test scores means the model learned the training rows too closely and does not generalise.

check.prompt: What does 5-fold cross-validation give you that a single split does not?

options.text: Five scores, so you see the average and how much it varies
A bigger training set for the final model
A way to skip the test set

check.explanation: Each fold is tested once, so you get five scores. Their mean is steadier than one split, and their spread shows how much the result depends on luck.

review_cards.back: TP / (TP + FP): of what the model flagged, the share that was right.
TP / (TP + FN): of what should have been found, the share that was found.
A high training score with a much lower test score.
Comparing models and choosing settings on the training data, with a mean and spread of scores, while the test set stays untouched.
